strengths: Resolves a well-motivated open question (whether a finite, polynomial-in-d regret bound is achievable in online inverse linear optimization) for the broad and practically relevant class of M-convex action sets, improving the prior finite bound of exp(O(d log d)) to O(d log d).

The technical approach is elegant and clearly explained: it combines a clean structural characterization of optimality on M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem, and the warm-up O(d^2) algorithm nicely motivates the refined O(d log d) result before adding complexity.

The extension to adversarial corruption is a nice addition: the paper gives a corruption-robust bound of O((C+1) d log d) without requiring knowledge of C, using an elegant cycle-detection/restart mechanism on the induced directed graphs (Lemma 5.1, 5.2), with intuitive illustrative examples (Figure 2).

A matching (up to log d) Ω(d) lower bound is established for the M-convex setting, by embedding the general lower-bound construction of Sakaue et al. (2025b) into an M-convex instance via the M♮-convex to M-convex embedding, showing the upper bound is nearly tight.

The paper is well organized, proofs are rigorous and mostly self-contained, and the exposition carefully explains intuition (e.g., the mistake-bound argument, the role of M-convexity, and why curved action sets are trivial).
weaknesses: The contribution is restricted to M-convex action sets, a significant restriction relative to the general polyhedral/combinatorial feasible sets studied in prior work (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Sakaue et al. 2025b); the paper does not fully clarify how large a gap remains between M-convex and general settings, nor whether the techniques could partially extend beyond M-convexity.

No experimental or empirical validation is provided; all results are purely theoretical, and there is no illustration of how the O(d log d) bound behaves in practice or how tight the constants are, which limits practical assessment of significance.

The computational complexity of the algorithm is not fully practical: exact computation of the center of gravity is #P-hard, requiring an approximate randomized algorithm (Lovász and Vempala) whose own approximation-induced regret degradation is not rigorously analyzed in the main text (only briefly mentioned in a footnote), leaving a gap between the idealized regret bound and what an implementable algorithm would achieve.

The corruption model (simple count C of suboptimal rounds) is more restrictive than the cumulative suboptimality framework of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the authors acknowledge this is left as future work, but it somewhat limits the immediate applicability of the corruption-robust result.
The O(log d) gap between the O(d log d) upper bound and the Ω(d) lower bound is left open, and it's unclear from the current analysis whether this gap can be closed or is fundamental.

The novelty relative to prior work is somewhat incremental in places: the volume argument is explicitly borrowed from the contextual search/pricing literature (as the authors themselves note), and the restart-based corruption handling is conceptually similar to existing corruption-robust frameworks (e.g., Gupta et al. 2025), differing mainly in using M-convex structure for detection rather than maintaining parallel copies.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open question in online inverse linear optimization: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in dimension d is achievable, providing a positive partial answer for the broad class of M-convex action sets (which includes matroids and various combinatorial structures).

The technical approach is elegant: combining a known structural characterization of M-convex optimality (Proposition 2.4) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem yields a clean progression from an O(d^2) warm-up algorithm to the sharper O(d log d) bound.

The corruption-robust extension is a nice contribution: by monitoring acyclicity of a directed graph built from feedback, the algorithm detects corruption and restarts without needing prior knowledge of the corruption budget C, achieving O((C+1) d log d) regret.

A matching Ω(d) lower bound (adapted from prior work via an M-convex embedding of the hard instance) shows the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor, giving a fairly complete picture for this action-set class.

The paper is generally well organized, with clear illustrative examples (matroids, extensions to integer lattices), a helpful comparison table against prior regret bounds, and a fairly complete treatment of computational costs, tie-breaking, and even a small numerical experiment to substantiate practical relevance.
weaknesses: The contribution only partially resolves the stated open problem: results are restricted to the special (though broad) class of M-convex action sets, not the general polyhedral/combinatorial feasible sets considered in prior work (Gollapudi et al., Sakaue et al.), so the core open question for general action sets remains unresolved.

The main technical tool (the volume/Grünbaum argument) is explicitly borrowed from the contextual search/pricing literature (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Paes Leme and Schneider 2022); the paper's novelty is mainly in combining this with the known M-convex exchange characterization, which, while useful, is a comparatively incremental synthesis rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Computing the exact center of gravity used for the sharper O(d log d) bound is #P-hard, and the polynomial-time approximate implementation described in the appendix has very high overhead (roughly O(d^6 log d · log T) per round), raising concerns about the practical usability of the refined algorithm despite its favorable asymptotic regret.
The Ω(log d) gap between the O(d log d) upper bound and the Ω(d) lower bound is left open, and it is unclear whether this gap can be closed, tempering the tightness claim.

Empirical validation is very limited: a single small synthetic experiment with time-varying uniform matroids (d=20) is reported, which is insufficient to assess robustness of the theoretical gains across richer M-convex structures (e.g., graphic matroids, integer-lattice extensions) or to validate the corruption-robust algorithm's practical performance under adversarial corruption.

The treatment of tied components in w*, while carefully discussed in the appendix, reveals that the corruption-detection mechanism fundamentally relies on strict distinctness of objective components, which may be a nontrivial assumption in practice and is not required in competing approaches (e.g., Sakaue et al. 2025b's O(d log T) bound handles corruption without such an assumption).
